pistillode.plain: A pistillode is a reduced, nonfunctional pistil left in a flower that functions as male.
pistillode.where: Look in the center of a staminate flower. If a small sterile gynoecium remains among the functional stamens, it is a pistillode.
pistillode.why: Pistillodes are useful when comparing male and female flowers in dioecious or otherwise unisexual species.

real_photo.label: Scientific illustration showing a pistillode in a staminate flower
real_photo.credit: Pedro Acevedo-Rodríguez · CC BY 4.0 / CC BY 3.0
real_photo.alt: Scientific botanical illustration of Allophylastrum frutescens including a staminate flower, nectary disc, stamens and pistillode
real_photo.focus: Use the staminate-flower detail and the separate pistillode drawing in the source plate. The reduced central gynoecium is the pistillode.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the PhytoKeys scientific illustration; the source explicitly labels the pistillode.

coriaceous.plain: Coriaceous means thick, firm, and leathery in texture.
coriaceous.formal: Having the texture or consistency of leather.
coriaceous.where: Observe a mature leaf’s thickness, stiffness, and durable surface rather than judging color alone.
coriaceous.why: Leathery versus thin or papery foliage is a useful vegetative character in many woody plants.

real_photo.label: Thick coriaceous Diospyros leaves
real_photo.alt: Real photograph of Diospyros maritima showing thick leathery coriaceous leaves
real_photo.focus: The blades are thick and firm rather than thin and papery. That leathery consistency is coriaceous.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to a Wikimedia Commons image specifically titled for coriaceous leaves.

distichous.plain: Distichous means leaves are arranged in two ranks along opposite sides of a stem or twig, forming one broad plane.
distichous.formal: Arranged in two ranks in a single plane.
distichous.where: Look down the length of a leafy twig rather than at a single node and see whether the leaves line up into two rows.
distichous.why: Two-ranked twig architecture is a useful whole-plant clue in elms and several unrelated groups.

real_photo.label: American elm twig with distichous leaf arrangement
real_photo.alt: Real photograph of Ulmus americana showing leaves arranged in two ranks along a twig
real_photo.focus: The leaves appear in two rows along opposite sides of the twig, producing a flattened two-ranked architecture.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to a Wikimedia Commons photograph whose source description explicitly notes distichous leaves.

oblique-base.plain: An oblique leaf base is asymmetric: one side of the blade reaches farther down toward the petiole than the other.
oblique-base.formal: A leaf base whose two sides are unequal or offset.
oblique-base.where: Ignore the leaf tip and focus only on the point where the blade meets the petiole.
oblique-base.why: A strongly uneven leaf base is a classic field clue for many elms.

real_photo.label: American elm leaf with an oblique base
real_photo.alt: Real photograph of Ulmus americana leaves showing asymmetric oblique leaf bases
real_photo.focus: At the blade base, one side extends lower than the other. That offset base is oblique.
real_photo.annotation_note: Same Wikimedia Commons elm photograph as the Distichous lesson, with the overlay focused on the asymmetric leaf base.

serrate.plain: Serrate means the leaf edge has sharp saw-like teeth pointing generally toward the tip.
serrate.formal: Bearing sharp marginal teeth directed toward the leaf apex.
serrate.where: Look closely along the blade margin and follow the direction of the tooth tips.
serrate.why: Margin type is a common key character and helps separate similar trees, shrubs, and herbs.

real_photo.label: Serrate leaf margin
real_photo.alt: Real close photograph of a Lantana camara leaf showing a serrate margin
real_photo.focus: Each sharp tooth along the edge points generally toward the leaf tip, producing the serrate saw-like margin.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the CC0 Wikimedia Commons photograph.

racemose.plain: Racemose describes an indeterminate flower-cluster pattern in which the main axis keeps growing while older flowers are lower and younger flowers are nearer the tip.
racemose.formal: An indeterminate inflorescence architecture with continued apical growth.
racemose.where: Follow the main flowering axis from bottom to top and compare the ages of the flowers or buds.
racemose.why: The flowering sequence helps distinguish racemose architecture from determinate cymose patterns.

real_photo.label: Real flowering raceme
real_photo.alt: Photograph of a flowering Maianthemum stellatum raceme
real_photo.focus: The main axis continues upward while lower flowers are older and upper flowers/buds are younger.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the existing LoJallen CC BY-SA 4.0 raceme photograph.

terminal-style.plain: A terminal style arises from the top of the ovary rather than from low between deeply divided ovary lobes.
terminal-style.formal: A style inserted apically on the ovary.
terminal-style.where: Move the corolla aside or use a dissected flower and trace the style to its point of origin on the ovary.
terminal-style.why: Terminal versus gynobasic style position is useful when separating lookalike flower architectures.

real_photo.label: Heliotropium flower with terminal style architecture
real_photo.alt: Real photograph of Heliotropium indicum, a species described as having a terminal style
real_photo.focus: The style arises from the top of the ovary rather than from between deeply divided lobes. Use the flower as a whole-plant anchor, then the definition for the exact internal position.
real_photo.annotation_note: The source description explicitly documents a terminal style; the ordinary field photograph cannot show the internal origin as clearly as a dissection.

annotations.label: STYLE ORIGIN IS AT OVARY TOP

didynamous.plain: Didynamous means a flower has four stamens arranged as two longer and two shorter.
didynamous.formal: An androecium of four stamens in two unequal pairs.
didynamous.where: Look inside the corolla and compare the heights of all four stamens rather than counting only the anthers.
didynamous.why: The two-long/two-short pattern is common in Lamiaceae and Verbenaceae and is a useful supporting character.

real_photo.label: Didynamous stamens — two long, two short
real_photo.alt: Scientific diagram showing four stamens arranged as two longer and two shorter
real_photo.focus: Two stamens extend farther than the other two. That 2+2 unequal arrangement is didynamous.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to a public-domain/CC0 scientific morphology diagram.

winged-seed.plain: A winged seed has thin papery extensions that increase surface area and help the seed travel on air.
winged-seed.formal: A seed bearing flattened membranous extensions that increase dispersal area.
winged-seed.where: Inspect naturally released seeds or mature opened capsules and distinguish the central seed body from the flat wing tissue.
winged-seed.why: Winged seeds are a strong clue in groups such as Bignoniaceae.

real_photo.label: Catalpa winged seeds
real_photo.alt: Real photograph of Catalpa bignonioides seeds showing broad papery wings and the central seed body
real_photo.focus: The slight thickening in the middle is the seed body; the broad flattened extensions are wings.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to a Wikimedia Commons photograph explicitly documented as winged Catalpa seeds.

stylopodium.plain: A stylopodium is the swollen or disk-like base of the styles sitting on top of the ovary in many Apiaceae.
stylopodium.formal: An expanded conical or disk-like base of the styles, often nectariferous, atop the ovary in Apiaceae.
stylopodium.where: Use a hand lens on a flower or young fruit. Find the two styles first, then look directly beneath them for the raised pad at the ovary top.
stylopodium.why: This style-base pad is a useful structural confirmation for Apiaceae and is often nectar-producing.

real_photo.label: Apiaceae flower diagram showing the stylopodium region
real_photo.alt: Public-domain diagram of an Apiaceae flower showing the top of the ovary and style bases
real_photo.focus: The swollen pad immediately beneath the styles and above the ovary is the stylopodium.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to a public-domain Apiaceae flower diagram.

interpetiolar-stipule.plain: An interpetiolar stipule sits between the petioles of an opposite leaf pair at the node.
interpetiolar-stipule.formal: A stipular structure occupying the node between opposite petiole bases.
interpetiolar-stipule.where: Find an opposite leaf pair, then look directly between the two petiole bases for a small flap, ridge, or bristle-like structure.
interpetiolar-stipule.why: Interpetiolar stipules are one of the strongest vegetative clues for many Rubiaceae.

real_photo.label: Rubiaceae interpetiolar stipule
real_photo.alt: Real close photograph of a Rubiaceae node showing an interpetiolar stipule between opposite petiole bases
real_photo.focus: The stipule lies directly between the two opposite petioles at the node.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to a Wikimedia Commons photograph explicitly documented as an interpetiolar stipule.

hilum.plain: The hilum is the scar on a seed marking where it was attached inside the fruit.
hilum.formal: The attachment scar marking the former connection between seed and funiculus/placenta.
hilum.where: Inspect a clean mature seed and look for an oval, linear, or differently colored scar on the seed coat.
hilum.why: Hilum size, position, and shape can be diagnostic in several plant groups.

real_photo.label: Seed diagram showing the hilum
real_photo.alt: Botanical diagram comparing monocot and dicot seeds with the hilum labeled on the dicot seed
real_photo.focus: On the dicot seed, the hilum marks the former point of attachment to the fruit.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to a Wikimedia Commons seed anatomy diagram that explicitly labels the hilum.

parallel-veined.plain: Parallel-veined leaves have major veins running side by side from near the base toward the tip.
parallel-veined.formal: Venation in which primary veins course approximately parallel through the blade.
parallel-veined.where: Hold the leaf flat or to the light and trace several major veins at once.
parallel-veined.why: Parallel venation strongly supports monocot identification when combined with other characters.

real_photo.label: Real leaf with parallel venation
real_photo.alt: Real photograph of a leaf showing major veins running approximately parallel through the blade
real_photo.focus: Trace several veins from the lower blade upward. They run alongside one another rather than forming a branching net.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the CC BY-SA 4.0 Wikimedia Commons photograph.

loculicidal.plain: Loculicidal means a capsule splits open through the middle of each chamber rather than along the partitions between chambers.
loculicidal.formal: Dehiscence along the dorsal suture or midline of each locule.
loculicidal.where: Look at a mature capsule and identify where the valves split relative to the internal locules.
loculicidal.why: The opening pattern is a useful technical fruit character in several families.

real_photo.label: Loculicidal capsule opening through the locule walls
real_photo.alt: Scientific diagram showing closed, opened, and cross-sectional views of a loculicidal capsule
real_photo.focus: The split runs down the back/middle of each locule, producing valves that open away from the internal partitions.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to a public-domain scientific fruit-morphology diagram.

anther-valve.plain: An anther valve is a small hinged flap of anther wall that lifts open to expose and release pollen.
anther-valve.formal: A valvular mode of anther dehiscence in which portions of the anther wall open as hinged flaps.
anther-valve.where: Use magnification on a mature Berberis-type anther and look for a flap opening upward rather than a slit or pore.
anther-valve.why: Valve-opening anthers are an unusually memorable character of Berberis and a few other groups.

real_photo.label: Berberis stamen with hinged anther valve
real_photo.alt: Public-domain botanical illustration of a Berberis vulgaris stamen with an anther valve lifted upward
real_photo.focus: The flap marked v in the source figure is an anther valve. It lifts away from the anther body and carries pollen on its inner surface.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to a public-domain botanical illustration explicitly showing an anther valve.

nectary.plain: A nectary is specialized tissue that produces nectar.
nectary.formal: A secretory organ or tissue producing nectar.
nectary.where: Look near the flower center or base of floral organs for a gland, ring, pad, cup, or other nectar-secreting structure.
nectary.why: Nectary shape and position can be useful floral characters and help explain pollinator behavior.

real_photo.label: Flower nectary with visible nectar
real_photo.alt: Real close photograph of a Chiranthodendron pentadactylon flower showing the nectary and abundant nectar
real_photo.focus: The nectar-producing tissue in the flower center is the nectary; the visible liquid is nectar produced by that tissue.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to a Wikimedia Commons photograph explicitly documented as showing a nectary and nectar.

hemiparasite.plain: A hemiparasite can photosynthesize for itself but still taps a host plant for water and dissolved nutrients.
hemiparasite.formal: A photosynthetic parasite obtaining water and/or solutes from a host through haustoria.
hemiparasite.where: Look for a green parasitic plant physically attached to a host stem or root system.
hemiparasite.why: The green foliage can make a hemiparasite look fully independent even though it is physiologically connected to a host.

real_photo.label: Phoradendron mistletoe hemiparasite on mesquite
real_photo.alt: Real photograph from Texas showing green Phoradendron tomentosum mistletoe growing on a Prosopis glandulosa host
real_photo.focus: The mistletoe is green and photosynthetic, but it is attached to the mesquite and draws water and solutes from it.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to a Texas Wikimedia Commons photograph whose source description explicitly identifies mistletoe as a hemiparasite.

haustorium.plain: A haustorium is the specialized organ a parasitic plant uses to penetrate host tissue and form a physiological connection.
haustorium.formal: A penetrative absorptive organ forming a physiological connection between parasite and host.
haustorium.where: The connection may be on stems or roots depending on the parasite. It is usually internal and should not be exposed by damaging plants.
haustorium.why: The haustorium is the actual feeding connection that makes plant parasitism possible.

real_photo.label: Mistletoe haustoria on a host branch
real_photo.alt: Real photograph of mistletoe haustorial structures attached to a Eucalyptus host
real_photo.focus: The swollen embedded connection between parasite and host marks the haustorial interface.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to a Wikimedia Commons photograph explicitly documented as mistletoe haustoria.

bract.plain: A bract is a modified leaf associated with a flower or flower cluster.
bract.formal: A foliar organ subtending a flower, branch, or inflorescence.
bract.where: Look directly beneath a flower or along the flowering axis for a leaf-like structure that is part of the reproductive display.
bract.why: Bracts can be more conspicuous than the true flowers, so learning to separate them prevents major ID mistakes.

real_photo.label: Bracts surrounding much smaller true flowers
real_photo.alt: Close photograph of Bougainvillea showing large purple bracts surrounding tiny white true flowers
real_photo.focus: The large purple structures are bracts. The tiny white structures nestled among them are the true flowers.
real_photo.annotation_note: Arrow/label overlay is added by the learner; the underlying Wikimedia Commons photograph is unmodified.

tendril.plain: A tendril is a slender coiling organ that wraps around nearby support and helps a vine climb.
tendril.formal: A modified stem, leaf, leaflet, or inflorescence specialized for climbing.
tendril.where: Inspect a vine node and follow the tendril back to its exact point of origin; that origin can help identify the plant group.
tendril.why: Tendril placement and structure can separate vines such as Passiflora, Vitis and Parthenocissus.

real_photo.label: Coiling Passiflora tendril
real_photo.alt: Real photograph of a Passiflora edulis tendril coiling around support
real_photo.focus: The thin curling structure is the tendril. It coils around support rather than functioning as a normal leaf blade.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the CC0 Wikimedia Commons photograph.

androgynophore.plain: An androgynophore is the stalk in the center of a flower that raises both the stamens and the ovary together above the perianth.
androgynophore.formal: An elongate floral axis bearing both androecium and gynoecium above the perianth.
androgynophore.where: In a passionflower, look above the corona for the central column supporting the anthers and ovary.
androgynophore.why: It is one of the most striking and memorable Passiflora structural features.

real_photo.label: Passiflora androgynophore in close-up
real_photo.alt: Real close photograph of Passiflora caerulea showing the central androgynophore
real_photo.focus: The central stalk lifts the anthers and ovary above the rest of the flower. That stalk is the androgynophore.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to a Wikimedia Commons macro explicitly documented as an androgynophore.

aril.plain: An aril is a fleshy or otherwise specialized covering that grows around part or all of a seed.
aril.formal: An accessory seed covering arising from the funiculus or seed attachment region.
aril.where: Inspect a mature seed inside an opened fruit and distinguish the seed coat from any extra fleshy covering attached around it.
aril.why: Arils often attract animals and can be useful diagnostic seed structures.

real_photo.label: Seed with fleshy aril
real_photo.alt: Real photograph of Chisocheton cumingianus fruit showing a seed surrounded by aril tissue
real_photo.focus: The fleshy tissue surrounding the seed is the aril; the hard seed itself lies inside that covering.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to a Wikimedia Commons photograph documented as showing aril and seed.

leaf-opposed.plain: Leaf-opposed means a structure arises directly across the stem from a leaf instead of from the leaf axil.
leaf-opposed.formal: Inserted on the node opposite a leaf.
leaf-opposed.where: At a node, find the leaf first and then look straight across the stem for the inflorescence or tendril.
leaf-opposed.why: This positional relationship is a useful field clue in several vine families, especially Vitaceae.

real_photo.label: Leaf-opposed flower clusters
real_photo.alt: Real photograph of Polygala paniculata showing racemes positioned opposite leaves
real_photo.focus: At each relevant node, the flower cluster sits across the stem from the leaf rather than in its axil.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to a Wikimedia Commons photograph whose source description explicitly states that the racemes are leaf-opposed.

annotations.label: ACROSS THE STEM, NOT IN AXIL

calyptra.plain: In grape flowers, the calyptra is the cap formed when the petals remain joined and detach together as one piece.
calyptra.formal: A cap or hood formed by coherent floral parts; in Vitis the petals may detach together as a calyptra.
calyptra.where: Look at opening Vitis flowers. Closed buds retain the petal cap, while newly opened flowers may show the cap lifting or already shed.
calyptra.why: This petal-cap mechanism is a distinctive feature of grape flowers.

real_photo.label: Grape flowers and closed buds with petal caps
real_photo.alt: Real photograph of Vitis vinifera flowers with some closed buds showing the coherent petal cap before it detaches
real_photo.focus: On the closed buds, the petals form a coherent cap. In Vitis that cap comes off together as the calyptra.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to a Wikimedia Commons grape-flower photograph showing both open flowers and closed buds.

triplinerved.plain: Triplinerved means three strong primary veins arise from or very near the base of the leaf.
triplinerved.formal: Bearing three prominent primary veins originating basally or subbasally.
triplinerved.where: Start at the petiole and trace the three most prominent veins upward through the blade.
triplinerved.why: This venation pattern is especially useful in hackberries and several other woody plants.

real_photo.label: Leaf showing three strong basal veins
real_photo.alt: Real photograph of Cryptocarya triplinervis leaves showing three prominent veins arising near the leaf base
real_photo.focus: Trace the midrib and the two strong side veins that start near the leaf base. Together they make the blade triplinerved.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the CC0 Wikimedia Commons photograph.

cystolith.plain: A cystolith is a mineral body, commonly calcium carbonate, formed inside a specialized plant cell.
cystolith.formal: A mineralized intracellular body, commonly calcium carbonate, associated with specialized epidermal cells.
cystolith.where: This is normally a microscopic character. In some leaves it contributes to a rough or dotted-looking surface, but confirmation usually requires magnification.
cystolith.why: Cystoliths are useful supporting anatomical characters in families such as Cannabaceae and Moraceae.

real_photo.label: Real cystolith inside Ficus epidermal cells
real_photo.alt: Microscope photograph of a cystolith formed in epidermal cells of Ficus elastica
real_photo.focus: The pale mineralized body inside the specialized epidermal cell is the cystolith.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the CC BY-SA 4.0 microscope photograph; the source explicitly documents a cystolith in Ficus elastica.

retinaculum.plain: A retinaculum is a stiff hook-like outgrowth inside many Acanthaceae capsules that supports a seed and helps fling it away when the fruit opens.
retinaculum.formal: A modified funicular or placental structure associated with seed support and release in Acanthaceae.
retinaculum.where: Inspect a naturally opened mature capsule. Look beneath the former seed positions for small rigid hook-like projections from the capsule wall.
retinaculum.why: Retinacula are one of the strongest fruit-level family characters for Acanthaceae.

real_photo.label: Acanthaceae capsule with exserted retinacula
real_photo.alt: Real macro photograph of a dehisced Barleria macrostegia capsule showing exserted retinacula and a seed
real_photo.focus: The rigid projections extending from the opened capsule valves are retinacula. They supported the seeds before explosive release.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the CC BY-SA 4.0 macro photograph; the source description explicitly identifies exserted retinacula.

perianth.plain: The perianth is the flower’s non-reproductive outer envelope: the sepals and petals together, or tepals when those two whorls are not clearly different.
perianth.formal: The collective calyx and corolla, or equivalent undifferentiated floral envelope.
perianth.where: Start at the outside of a flower and move inward until you reach the stamens and pistil. Everything floral before the reproductive organs is the perianth.
perianth.why: Perianth is the useful umbrella term when calyx and corolla are unusual, reduced, or not clearly distinguishable.

real_photo.label: Perianth = calyx + corolla
real_photo.alt: Learner flower diagram showing the calyx and corolla together as the perianth
real_photo.focus: The sepals/calyx plus the petals/corolla together make the perianth.
real_photo.annotation_note: Existing learner-created flower diagram reused to show the part-to-whole relationship.

gynostemium.plain: A gynostemium is a compact reproductive column formed where male and female floral tissues are closely united.
gynostemium.formal: A columnar floral structure formed by union or close association of androecial and gynoecial tissues.
gynostemium.where: In Aristolochia, look deep inside the flower tube at the reproductive column above the ovary.
gynostemium.why: It is a key structural feature for understanding Aristolochia flower architecture.

real_photo.label: Aristolochia cutaway with gynostemium labeled
real_photo.alt: Botanical cutaway drawing of Aristolochia grandiflora with the gynostemium identified as structure 2
real_photo.focus: Find source label 2 near the base of the flower tube. That compact reproductive column is the gynostemium.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to Carstor's Aristolochia cutaway; the source legend explicitly identifies structure 2 as the gynostemium.

areole.plain: An areole is the specialized cactus growth point that produces spines, hairs, branches, or flowers.
areole.formal: A highly specialized axillary bud/short-shoot structure diagnostic of Cactaceae.
areole.where: Look for repeated small cushions or pads on the cactus stem or cladode.
areole.why: Areoles are the defining structural feature of Cactaceae.

real_photo.label: Cactus areoles in close-up
real_photo.alt: Real close photograph of cactus areoles with spine clusters emerging from specialized cushion-like points
real_photo.focus: Each small cushion-like point from which the spines emerge is one areole.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the Wikimedia Commons close-up of cactus areoles.

glochid.plain: A glochid is a tiny barbed bristle produced in Opuntioideae areoles.
glochid.formal: A minute, readily detached, barbed spine characteristic of Opuntioideae.
glochid.where: Look closely at prickly-pear areoles without touching them. Glochids often form dense fuzzy-looking tufts among or around larger spines.
glochid.why: Glochids are a strong structural clue for prickly pears and their close relatives.

real_photo.label: Opuntia glochids at 20× magnification
real_photo.alt: Magnified real photograph of Opuntia areoles showing dense clusters of tiny barbed glochids and larger spines
real_photo.focus: The dense short golden-brown bristles are glochids. The much larger rigid structures are ordinary spines.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to a Wikimedia Commons macro explicitly documented as Opuntia glochids at 20× magnification.

cladode.plain: A cladode is a modified photosynthetic stem that looks and functions like a leaf.
cladode.formal: A modified photosynthetic stem or branch resembling a leaf.
cladode.where: On prickly pears, treat the flat pad itself as a stem segment and then look for areoles on its surface.
cladode.why: This prevents the common mistake of calling cactus pads leaves.

real_photo.label: Young Opuntia cladodes
real_photo.alt: Real photograph of young Opuntia cochenillifera cladodes
real_photo.focus: Each broad flat green pad is a cladode — a stem segment carrying areoles.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the Wikimedia Commons photograph explicitly identified as young cladodes.

succulent.plain: Succulent means a plant organ is thick and fleshy because it stores water.
succulent.formal: Water-storing vegetative tissue with enlarged parenchymatous organs.
succulent.where: Look for enlarged leaves or stems with substantial water-storage tissue.
succulent.why: Succulence is an ecological and anatomical trait, not a family by itself.

real_photo.label: Thick water-storing succulent leaves
real_photo.alt: Real close photograph of thick fleshy succulent leaves
real_photo.focus: The visibly thick, fleshy blades contain enlarged water-storage tissue.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to a Wikimedia Commons photograph of succulent leaves.

urceolate.plain: Urceolate means urn-shaped: swollen through the lower portion and narrowed toward the opening.
urceolate.formal: A sympetalous corolla shape resembling an urn or pitcher.
urceolate.where: View the flower from the side and compare the width of the middle with the narrower mouth.
urceolate.why: Urn-shaped corollas are common in several Ericaceae and are useful descriptive characters.

real_photo.label: Urceolate flower shape
real_photo.alt: Public-domain diagram of an urn-shaped urceolate corolla
real_photo.focus: The corolla is broader below and constricted near the opening, producing the urn-like shape.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to a public-domain flower-shape diagram.

poricidal.plain: Poricidal anthers release pollen through small pores rather than opening along long slits.
poricidal.formal: Dehiscing through terminal or subterminal pores.
poricidal.where: Use a hand lens or macro view at the anther tips and look for small terminal or subterminal openings.
poricidal.why: Poricidal anthers are strongly associated with buzz pollination in groups such as Solanum and many Ericaceae.

real_photo.label: Poricidal anthers in a buzz-pollinated Solanum
real_photo.alt: Macro photograph of a Solanum flower center showing anther cone with poricidal anthers
real_photo.focus: The pollen exits through small pores near the anther tips rather than through long side slits.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to a Wikimedia Commons photograph explicitly documented as showing poricidal anthers.

husk.plain: A husk is the outer fleshy, fibrous, or leathery covering around a nut or similar seed-bearing structure.
husk.formal: A fleshy, fibrous, or leathery outer fruit/perianth-derived layer surrounding a nut.
husk.where: On a walnut, look at the green-to-brown outer covering before reaching the hard shell of the nut.
husk.why: The fleshy outer husk around a hard nut is a familiar Juglandaceae fruit cue.

real_photo.label: Walnut with the outer husk split open
real_photo.alt: Real photograph of a common walnut with its outer husk split to reveal the hard nut inside
real_photo.focus: The split outer covering is the husk. The hard structure visible inside is the nut shell.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the CC BY-SA 2.5 Wikimedia Commons photograph.

chambered-pith.plain: Chambered pith is stem pith divided into a row of small compartments by transverse partitions.
chambered-pith.formal: Pith interrupted by transverse partitions or diaphragms.
chambered-pith.where: It is visible only in an appropriate cut or broken twig. In walnut, a longitudinal section reveals repeated internal chambers.
chambered-pith.why: Chambered pith is a useful secondary twig character for Juglans.

real_photo.label: Walnut twig with chambered pith
real_photo.alt: Real longitudinal view of a walnut twig showing pith divided into repeated chambers
real_photo.focus: The dark internal pith is interrupted by repeated transverse partitions, creating the chambered pattern.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the Wikimedia Commons photograph explicitly documented as walnut chambered pith.

annular-stipule-scar.plain: An annular stipule scar is a ring-like scar that completely encircles a twig after a sheathing stipule falls away.
annular-stipule-scar.formal: An encircling nodal scar produced by a sheathing stipule.
annular-stipule-scar.where: On a sycamore twig, inspect the node for a thin line running all the way around the twig.
annular-stipule-scar.why: A stipule scar that encircles the twig is a strong Platanus winter-twig character.

real_photo.label: Sycamore-style annular stipule scar
real_photo.alt: Learner diagram of a Platanus twig with a ring-like stipule scar encircling the twig
real_photo.focus: The pale ring runs all the way around the twig. That complete ring is the annular stipule scar.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner-created diagram based on the standard Platanus twig character; used because the thin ring is often difficult to isolate cleanly in ordinary photographs.

aliases: male and female flowers on one plant
monoecious.plain: Monoecious means one individual plant bears separate male and female flowers.
monoecious.formal: A sexual system in which staminate and pistillate flowers occur on the same individual.
monoecious.where: Inspect one flowering plant and look for two distinct flower types on that same individual.
monoecious.why: Monoecious plants separate male and female functions into different flowers without separating them onto different plants.

real_photo.label: Male and female flowers on the same Comptonia plant
real_photo.alt: Real photograph of Comptonia peregrina showing a male catkin above and a female flower below on the same plant
real_photo.focus: The catkin above is male and the red structure below is female. Both occur on the same individual plant.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the CC BY-SA 3.0 Wikimedia Commons photograph; the source description identifies both flower sexes.

stipe.plain: The stipe is the stalk of a fern frond below the leafy blade.
stipe.formal: The petiole-like basal stalk of a fern frond.
stipe.where: Follow a fern frond upward from the rhizome. The bare stalk below the first pinnae or blade divisions is the stipe.
stipe.why: Separating stipe from rachis gives you the basic framework for describing a fern frond.

real_photo.label: Fern frond with the stipe identified
real_photo.alt: Public-domain botanical line drawing illustrating the stipe as the basal stalk of a fern frond
real_photo.focus: On the fern example, the stalk below the leafy blade is the stipe. Above the first blade divisions, the continuing axis is the rachis.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to a public-domain Pearson Scott Foresman illustration whose source definition includes the petiole of a fern frond.

pinna.plain: A pinna is one primary division of a pinnate fern frond.
pinna.formal: A primary segment of a pinnate fern blade.
pinna.where: Look at the fern’s main rachis and identify the large repeated side divisions attached directly to it.
pinna.why: Once you can separate the whole frond from individual pinnae, fern descriptions become much easier to follow.

real_photo.label: Pinnate fern frond showing individual pinnae
real_photo.alt: Real photograph of a pinnate fern frond with repeated pinnae along the main rachis
real_photo.focus: Each large side division attached directly to the main rachis is one pinna.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to a GFDL Wikimedia Commons fern photograph.

pinnule.plain: A pinnule is a smaller secondary division within a pinna.
pinnule.formal: A secondary division of a pinnate fern frond.
pinnule.where: First identify a pinna, then look within it for the next repeated level of subdivision.
pinnule.why: Pinna versus pinnule is essential terminology when comparing more finely divided ferns.

real_photo.label: Fern pinnule with sori on its underside
real_photo.alt: Real close photograph of a Dryopteris dilatata pinnule showing sori on the underside
real_photo.focus: The entire small divided blade shown here is one pinnule. The brown reproductive clusters on it are sori.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the CC BY-SA 4.0 Wikimedia Commons photograph.

sorus.plain: A sorus is a cluster of many spore-producing sporangia on a fern.
sorus.formal: An aggregation of sporangia on a fern frond.
sorus.where: Usually turn a fertile frond over. Look for repeated dots, lines or marginal patches on the underside.
sorus.why: Sorus shape and position are among the most important fern-identification characters.

real_photo.label: Round sori on the underside of a fern frond
real_photo.alt: Real photograph of the underside of Polypodium vulgare showing many round sori
real_photo.focus: Each brown round cluster is one sorus. Each sorus contains many much smaller sporangia.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the Wikimedia Commons photograph.

sporangium.plain: A sporangium is one tiny capsule-like organ that produces and releases spores.
sporangium.where: Use magnification. A sorus is made of many individual sporangia packed together.
sporangium.why: Understanding sporangium versus sorus is the fern equivalent of understanding one floret versus a whole flower head.

real_photo.label: Fern sporangia under scanning electron microscopy
real_photo.alt: Scanning electron micrograph of fern sporangia in different stages of spore release
real_photo.focus: Each capsule-like body is one sporangium. Multiple sporangia are grouped together into a sorus on the fern.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the CC BY-SA 3.0 scanning electron micrograph.

false-indusium.plain: A false indusium is the rolled or folded edge of a fern blade that bends over and protects the sori.
false-indusium.formal: A recurved or modified laminar margin sheltering marginal sori, rather than a separate true indusial membrane.
false-indusium.where: Inspect the margin of a fertile maidenhair or cliffbrake-type fern from below. Look for the leaf edge itself folding over the reproductive structures.
false-indusium.why: This differs from a true indusium because the protective flap is made from the leaf margin rather than a separate membrane.

real_photo.label: Adiantum false indusium formed by the folded leaf margin
real_photo.alt: Real close photograph of an Adiantum false indusium where the leaf margin folds over the sori
real_photo.focus: The protective flap is actually the rolled leaf margin. That folded edge is the false indusium.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the CC BY 4.0 Wikimedia Commons photograph.

heterophylly.plain: Heterophylly means one plant produces noticeably different leaf forms, often because of developmental stage or environment.
heterophylly.formal: Production of morphologically distinct leaf types on the same individual, often in response to environment or developmental stage.
heterophylly.where: Compare leaves on the same individual, especially submerged versus emergent growth in aquatic plants.
heterophylly.why: Heterophylly can make one species look like two completely different plants if you only see one growth form.

real_photo.label: Heterophylly — submerged and emergent leaf forms
real_photo.alt: Real photograph of Hygrophila difformis showing different submerged and emergent leaf morphologies on the same species
real_photo.focus: Compare the finely divided submerged leaves with the thicker emergent leaves. The same species produces both forms.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the CC BY-SA 4.0 photograph; the source explicitly describes heterophylly between submerged and above-water growth.

phyllode.plain: A phyllode is a flattened photosynthetic petiole or leaf axis that takes over the job of a normal leaf blade.
phyllode.formal: A flattened photosynthetic petiole or modified leaf axis functioning in place of a conventional lamina.
phyllode.where: In classic Acacia examples, compare juvenile pinnately compound leaves with later flattened blade-like phyllodes.
phyllode.why: A phyllode may look like a simple leaf blade, but developmentally it is a modified petiole or leaf axis.

real_photo.label: Acacia transition from compound leaf to phyllode
real_photo.alt: Real photograph of Acacia melanoxylon juvenile growth showing transitional leaves from pinnately compound blades to phyllodes
real_photo.focus: Compare the compound juvenile leaf with the flattened blade-like structure. The flattened structure is the phyllode.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the CC BY-SA 4.0 photograph; the source explicitly documents the transition from compound blade to phyllode.

enantiostyly.plain: Enantiostyly is floral handedness: some flowers deflect the style to one side and others mirror that arrangement to the opposite side.
enantiostyly.formal: A floral polymorphism in which reproductive organs are reciprocally deflected to opposite sides in different flowers.
enantiostyly.where: Compare multiple flowers face-on and look at the relative side occupied by the style versus the major pollinating stamens.
enantiostyly.why: The reciprocal left/right arrangement helps position pollen and stigmas on different parts of a visiting pollinator.

real_photo.label: Mirror-image left- and right-styled flowers
real_photo.alt: Learner diagram comparing two mirror-image floral morphs with the style and stamens deflected to opposite sides
real_photo.focus: The style switches from one side to the other between floral morphs, while major stamens occupy the reciprocal side.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner-created diagram used because enantiostyly is fundamentally a comparison between two floral morphs and is clearer side-by-side than in a single photograph.

salverform.plain: Salverform means the corolla has a long or narrow tube that abruptly opens into a flat spreading limb.
salverform.formal: A sympetalous corolla with an elongated narrow tube and abruptly spreading limb.
salverform.where: View the flower from the side: trace the narrow tube, then notice the sudden flat expansion at the top.
salverform.why: Corolla shape is an important comparative character across many sympetalous families.

real_photo.label: Salverform corolla — narrow tube with flat limb
real_photo.alt: Real close photograph of Brunfelsia australis flowers showing a short narrow corolla tube and flat spreading limb
real_photo.focus: The flower has a narrow tube that opens abruptly into a flat five-lobed face.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to a Wikimedia Commons image whose source description explicitly calls the flower salverform.

staminate.plain: A staminate flower functions as male: it has functional stamens and no functional pistil.
staminate.formal: A unisexual flower bearing functional stamens and lacking a functional gynoecium.
staminate.where: Look for pollen-bearing anthers and compare the center with a pistillate flower of the same species.
staminate.why: Recognizing staminate flowers helps you read unisexual plants and understand male-versus-female reproductive roles.

real_photo.label: Staminate Sassafras flower
real_photo.alt: Real comparison photograph showing a male Sassafras flower with multiple stamens
real_photo.focus: Use the flower on the left. Its conspicuous stamens and anthers make it staminate.
real_photo.annotation_note: Same CC BY-SA 3.0 Sassafras comparison photo as the Dioecious lesson, focused on the male flower.

pistillate.plain: A pistillate flower functions as female: it has a functional pistil and no functional stamens.
pistillate.formal: A unisexual flower bearing a functional gynoecium and lacking functional stamens.
pistillate.where: Look for the central stigma/style/ovary structure and compare it with a staminate flower of the same species.
pistillate.why: Pistillate flowers develop the fruit after successful pollination.

real_photo.label: Pistillate Sassafras flower
real_photo.alt: Real comparison photograph showing a female Sassafras flower with a central pistil
real_photo.focus: Use the flower on the right. Its central pistil is the functional female reproductive structure.
real_photo.annotation_note: Same CC BY-SA 3.0 Sassafras comparison photo as the Dioecious lesson, focused on the female flower.

pollinarium.plain: The whole milkweed pollen-transfer unit, usually two pollinia linked by connecting arms to a small central clip.
pollinarium.formal: A pollen-transfer complex consisting of pollinia connected by translator arms to a corpusculum.
pollinarium.where: Look at the tiny removable pollen apparatus associated with the stigmatic slits of a milkweed gynostegium.
pollinarium.why: It explains how milkweed pollen is removed and transferred as a single mechanical unit rather than loose grains.

real_photo.label: Real Asclepias asperula pollinarium
real_photo.alt: Macro photograph of Asclepias asperula pollinarium
real_photo.focus: The whole structure — two pollinia, translator arms, and the central corpusculum — is one pollinarium.
real_photo.annotation_note: Learner overlay is added to the existing Auracas CC BY-SA 4.0 macro photograph.

corpusculum.plain: The tiny central clip-like part of a milkweed pollinarium that catches on a pollinator.
corpusculum.formal: The central hardened body of the pollinarium that connects translator arms leading to the pollinia.
corpusculum.where: Look at the center of a detached milkweed pollinarium between the two pollen masses.
corpusculum.why: It is the mechanical attachment point that helps a pollinator pull the pollinarium from the flower.

real_photo.label: Pollinarium showing the central corpusculum

raceme.plain: A raceme is an unbranched flower cluster with individual flowers on short stalks along one main axis.
raceme.formal: An indeterminate, unbranched inflorescence bearing pedicellate flowers along an elongated main axis.
raceme.where: Trace the flower cluster from bottom to top and look for one main axis with separate flower stalks coming off its sides.
raceme.why: Recognizing a raceme helps separate one common inflorescence architecture from spikes, panicles, umbels and heads.
